raw_response:
I’m 63 this year. My old man and I have farmed these 14 mu for over 30 years. We never went to school, not one day, but we know this land better than any book. We know the east plot stays wet longer after rain, and the south plot near the road has better soil.

Last year was an okay year. Our wheat gave us about 800 jin per mu — not great, not bad. The maize after wheat was about 850 jin per mu. The cotton on our 4 mu, we got roughly 1,000 jin of seed cotton per mu. We didn’t lose money, and that’s what matters.

This year, I don’t want to try anything new. New things are for young people with money to burn. We’re old now, and there’s only the two of us. Our son works in the city and sends money sometimes, but we can’t use that for farming — that’s for emergencies.

The wheat went in last October, same as always. We used our own saved seed, bought a little extra from the shop to fill in. Before planting, we spread one bag of that compound fertilizer per mu — the kind the shop calls 15-15-15, though I just know it as the white bag with blue writing. Now it’s April, the wheat is up and green. I need to spread urea soon, about half a bag per mu, before we turn on the water. Old Wang down the road uses more fertilizer than us, but I think our wheat looks fine. We’ll water three times total — we already did the winter water in November, now we need to water at jointing, and once more when the grain is filling.

The maize goes in right after wheat harvest in mid-June. We never have much time — usually the combine cuts the wheat, and within a day or two we plant the maize. We buy hybrid seed from the shop, the red bag, costs about 50 yuan per mu. One bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, then when the maize is knee-high, we spread some urea — maybe one-third of a bag per mu. Water twice if the rain doesn’t come. We hire Old Zhang’s tractor for planting if our old machine breaks down.

Cotton is hard work, but we keep 4 mu. It brings good money if the price holds. We plant in the next week or two when the soil warms up. We make proper beds — plow and ridge it. Cotton needs clean fields, so we spray herbicide. We fertilize twice: some compound fertilizer at planting, then urea when the flowers come. The problem is picking. Our backs hurt after one hour of bending. Last year we hired women from the village to help pick in September and October. We’ll need to do that again this year, probably more because my knees are getting worse. That’s the biggest cost for cotton, but without hired pickers, the cotton stays in the field.

Money is always tight. We have about 15,000 yuan saved for this year’s inputs. Seeds, fertilizer, water, and the pickers for cotton — it all adds up. Two years ago we tried to save money by buying less fertilizer. The wheat turned yellow and thin. We lost more in yield than we saved on those bags. Now I always put a little more rather than less. Better to waste some fertilizer than to lose a whole crop.

The spring has been dry, so I’ll watch the wheat closely. I don’t trust the weather reports on the phone — I watch the clouds and talk to my neighbors. If Old Wang waters his wheat tomorrow, I water mine the day after.
